common_name: Staro Chives (Thick-Leaf Freezing and Drying Cultivar)

planting.note: Direct sow or start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost, or plant divisions of an established clump in spring; Staro's heavier leaf tissue was bred specifically to hold up through commercial freezing and drying, which also makes it a strong choice for home gardeners who preserve a bulk harvest.

directions: Staro is a European market-garden chive selection bred for thicker, larger leaf blades than standard chives, a trait developed so the harvested leaf holds its color, texture, and flavor after freezing or dehydrating rather than turning limp or discolored. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and harvest by cutting outer leaves close to the base every few weeks to keep the clump producing tender new growth. The heavier leaf structure also makes Staro easier to chop cleanly for fresh use than the thinner-leaved standard chive types. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to renew vigor and prevent the center of the clump from dying out.
sources: Cornell University Herb Garden reference collection

planting.note: Plant divisions of an established clump in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this dwarf form stays compact and is well suited to rock gardens, edging, and container culture rather than large-scale kitchen production.

directions: Corsican White is a very dwarf, fine-textured chive selection originally collected as wild seed from Corsica and later named for its distinctive pure white flower globes, a color break from the usual lilac-pink of common chives. Its narrow leaves and slender stems are noticeably sparser and shorter than standard chives, making it better suited to small edging, rock garden, or container plantings than to bulk culinary harvest. Grow in full sun in gritty, well-drained soil, since the compact habit is prone to being overwhelmed by competing foliage in rich, damp beds. Divide clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the tight, tidy mound from thinning out, and shear off spent flower heads to tidy the display once bloom fades.
sources: Pacific Bulb Society wiki — Allium schoenoprasum forms
specialty perennial nursery cultivar records (e.g. Digging Dog Nursery, Plant Delights Nursery)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Snowcap forms a low mound of fine, gray-green foliage topped by rounded white blooms, making it as much a border and rock-garden ornamental as a kitchen herb.

directions: Snowcap is a semi-dwarf chive selection bred for its pristine white, tightly spherical flower heads held just above a low, mounding clump of finely textured, gray-green leaves, a striking contrast to the lilac-pink blooms of ordinary chives. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained soil, where the compact habit performs well as edging or in rock gardens without sprawling into neighboring plants. Snip leaves regularly for the same mild onion flavor as standard chives, and shear back spent flower stalks after bloom to encourage a tidy second flush of foliage. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain the tight, uniform mound this cultivar is prized for.
sources: specialty perennial and allium nursery cultivar records (e.g. Stonehouse Nursery, Digging Dog Nursery)
North American Rock Garden Society — Allium species and cultivar notes

planting.note: Direct sow or start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost, or plant divisions in spring; Kobold's compact, uniform habit was selected specifically for balconies, containers, and small raised beds where standard garlic chives would sprawl too wide.

directions: Kobold is a compact, uniform garlic chive selection bred with thin, aromatic, flat stems and a noticeably tighter growth habit than standard Allium tuberosum, which typically sprawls wider and taller. This scaled-down footprint makes Kobold well suited to container culture, window boxes, and small kitchen-garden beds where standard garlic chives would quickly outgrow the space. Grow in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, and harvest the flat, garlic-flavored leaves regularly by cutting near the base to encourage steady regrowth. Deadhead the white star-shaped flower clusters after bloom if self-seeding is a concern, since garlic chives can spread readily from seed even in a compact cultivar.
sources: European perennial herb nursery cultivar catalogs (e.g. Ballyrobert Gardens)

planting.note: Plant rooted slips 2-5 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; Ginseng Red is a semi-bush heirloom with a cut-leaf habit, kept in circulation by a Virginia family for over four decades before wider seed-saver distribution.

directions: Ginseng Red is a semi-bush heirloom sweet potato with a distinctive cut, lobed leaf and pinkish-red skin over light orange flesh, an early-maturing variety long grown by a Virginia farm family before it entered wider seed-saver circulation. Its more restrained, semi-bush vine habit takes up less garden space than sprawling standard sweet potato varieties, making it a reasonable choice for smaller plots. Plant slips in full sun in loose, well-drained soil after the danger of frost has passed, and hill soil lightly around the base as vines establish to encourage even root development. After harvest, cure roots for about a week at warm temperatures and high humidity, then continue storing them for several additional weeks, since growers report the flavor and sweetness of Ginseng Red noticeably improve the longer it is kept in storage.
sources: Sand Hill Preservation Center sweet potato variety descriptions
Dave's Garden PlantFiles — Ipomoea batatas 'Ginseng Red'

common_name: Ginseng Orange Sweet Potato (Orange-Fleshed Sport of Ginseng Red)

planting.note: Plant rooted slips 2-5 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; Ginseng Orange is a naturally occurring orange-skinned, orange-fleshed sport discovered within Ginseng Red plantings, sharing the same early, semi-bush, cut-leaf habit as its parent.

directions: Ginseng Orange is a color-sport selection derived from the Virginia heirloom Ginseng Red, retaining the same early maturity, semi-bush vine habit, and cut, lobed leaf, but with orange skin and orange flesh in place of Ginseng Red's pinkish-red skin and light orange flesh. Its compact, semi-bush growth is well suited to smaller garden beds where a fully sprawling vine variety would be unwelcome. Set slips in full sun in loose, fertile, well-drained soil after the last frost, keeping the row lightly hilled as vines fill in to protect developing roots from sun exposure and cracking. Growers note this variety produces reliably above-average yields for an heirloom type; cure roots for about a week in warm, humid conditions after digging to firm the skin and improve storage life before moving them to cooler, drier long-term storage.
sources: Sand Hill Preservation Center sweet potato variety descriptions
